html:
A soft robot that crawls through the small intestine like a snake; robots that copy themselves; the robotics radar.
TECH RADAR
A soft robot that crawls deep into the gut, where today's instruments struggle to reach
No. 9 · Friday 30 October 2026 · Robotics and automation · 6 min read
 
IN 30 SECONDS
1Researchers at Harvard and MIT built a soft, snake-inspired robot that travelled 2 metres along a pig's small intestine in 11 minutes, with a channel for medical tools.
2A person-following robot that predicts where you went after a corner completes 87% of its tasks, against 55% for the standard method.
3Robotics radar: research grows faster this year than in the previous three, and new humanoid-robot projects on GitHub nearly tripled in a year.
247
new robotics papers today
+32%
robotics research momentum this year compared with all research
+182%
new GitHub projects on humanoid robots, Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025
SIGNAL OF THE DAY
BIOSENTER: a soft robot that moves, steers and works inside the small intestine
Science Robotics · 28 October  Journal  High-impact journal
Who wrote it: Binbin Ying and 11 others · Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard University, Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research at MIT (United States) · among the authors Giovanni Traverso, h-index 66
Context. The small intestine is several metres long, narrow and full of bends. Standard endoscopes struggle to reach its deeper parts, which makes bleeding, inflammation and tumours there hard to diagnose and treat.
The robot is a soft tube moved by air. Its head and tail inflate and grip the intestinal wall through sleeves cut like paper art (kirigami), while the body stretches forward and bends in any direction, much like a snake or an inchworm. A central channel lets doctors pass the usual endoscopic tools. Each end grips with a force of about 1.5 newtons, roughly the weight of a small apple. In tests on pigs it travelled 2 metres along the collapsed, winding small intestine in 11 minutes, pushing gently with 2.2 to 6.4 newtons. It is today's signal because it brings the advantages of soft robots, gentle and flexible, to a medical need that rigid instruments serve poorly.
PAPERS OF THE DAY · ROBOTICS AND AUTOMATION
Robot path planninggrowing
Research share +42% in 3 years · 3,158 papers in 2025
What it is about. How a robot decides where to move, step by step, without bumping into things or people.
Belief-integrated timed elastic band planning for robust indoor person following under intermittent observations
Scientific Reports · 26 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Jian Guan and 4 others · East China University of Science and Technology (China) · among the authors Wei Hu, h-index 30
CONTEXTRobots that follow a person, carrying luggage in an airport or tools in a hospital, lose sight of them at corners, doors and in crowds, and usually stop where they last saw them.
WHAT THEY DOThe robot keeps an estimate of where the hidden person is probably going and plans its route on that guess, actively searching likely paths.
RESULTIn 4,320 simulated runs across eight indoor scenes it completed 87.36% of following tasks, against 55.14% for the standard planner, and missed its 100-millisecond control deadline least often (3.32% of cycles).
WHY IT MATTERSFollowing people reliably indoors is a basic skill for service robots in shops, hospitals and homes. Tested in simulation only.
Robot manipulation and learningstrong growth
Research share +62% in 3 years · 3,118 papers in 2025
What it is about. Robots that grasp and handle objects; today's growth comes from robots that learn these skills and work side by side with people.
Design and simulation of an interactive human robot disassembly system for end of life phones
Frontiers in Robotics and AI · 27 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Soufiane Ameur and 4 others · Arts et Métiers, École Marocaine des Sciences de l'Ingénieur, Laboratoire d'Ingénierie des Systèmes Physiques et Numériques (France, Morocco) · among the authors Mohamed Tabaa, h-index 22
CONTEXTOld phones contain valuable materials, but taking them apart by hand is slow and taking them apart only with robots is hard, because every model is different.
WHAT THEY DOA recycling line with six stations where robots and workers share the job; workers can reassign tasks or fix errors by voice or hand gestures.
RESULTIn simulation, a batch of 10 phones takes about 95.5 seconds per phone, with error rates of 3.3% to 4.1%; hand gestures are recognised with confidence of 0.91 to 0.94.
WHY IT MATTERSElectronic waste keeps growing: combining robots with human judgement could make recovering materials affordable. Still a simulation and a proof of concept.
Modular robots and swarmsstable
Research share +1% in 3 years · 284 papers in 2025
What it is about. Robots made of identical blocks that can connect into different shapes, like smart building bricks.
Robotic Budding: From Homogeneous Cells to Diverse Morphologies in Physical Self-Reproduction
arXiv · 22 October  Preprint – not peer reviewed  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Siyuan Zhang and 3 others · among the authors Hod Lipson (Columbia University), h-index 76
WHAT THEY DOA single type of module with magnetic connectors and two motorised joints, which folds from flat into 3D shapes. An assembled robot, steered by a person, collects spare modules and builds an identical copy of itself, which then detaches: a kind of 'budding', as in some plants and animals.
WHY IT MATTERSAn early but striking step towards machines that build and repair themselves. Preliminary demonstrations, still controlled by a human, and not yet peer reviewed.
RADAR OF THE DAY · ROBOTICS AND AUTOMATION
What it is about. Machines that sense their surroundings and act in the physical world: factory arms, warehouse robots, self-driving vehicles, medical robots. The big change is that robots increasingly learn from examples and experience instead of being programmed step by step.

cars and vehicles that drive themselves, and how to make them safe

choosing routes that avoid obstacles and people

What developers and the public do
SIGNALGITHUB
(year on year)		HACKER NEWS
(year on year)
«humanoid robot»▲ +182%▲ +115%
«robot learning»▲ +146%▼ −20%
GitHub: new projects; Hacker News: stories discussed (only 8 for robot learning). Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025; for comparison, all new GitHub projects grew 62% and Hacker News discussions fell 38%. Wikipedia, 12 months: views down for humanoid robots (−18%), self-driving cars (−39%) and industrial robots (−22%). Data updated 27 October.
In short: Researchers and developers move together, especially on humanoids and robots that learn, and humanoids are the only robotics topic discussed more than a year ago; general public curiosity, measured on Wikipedia, keeps falling.
WORDS OF THE DAY
h-index — a measure of how often a researcher is cited: an h-index of 50 means 50 papers cited at least 50 times each. Above 40 usually indicates an established name in the field.
Soft robot — a robot made of flexible materials such as silicone, often moved by air, which can squeeze and bend like an octopus arm.
Endoscope — a thin flexible tube with a camera that doctors pass into the body to look inside and treat problems.
WORTH WATCHING
Tomorrow the weekend overview compares all five verticals. Worth watching: the first human trials of soft robots like today's signal, the step that will show whether they can reach the clinic.

How to read: takeaways come only from the abstracts; "Why it matters" is Claude's reading. Labels say whether a paper has been peer reviewed; "High-impact journal" and "Who wrote it" come from OpenAlex citation statistics. OpenAlex does not check the content.
Several of today's results come from simulations or animal tests, and one paper is a preprint. A journal's quality does not guarantee that results are correct.
